newsitem.title: USA: Conn. monitor faults how gov would spend surplus.
newsitem.headline: Conn. monitor faults how gov would spend surplus.

text.p: Connecticut's comptroller on Friday faulted how Gov. John Rowland's plans for spending an estimated $120 million surplus, saying the proposal would result in long-term budget gaps.

"The proposal will create long-term, structural state deficits including, according to the governor's own projections, a $163 million deficit in fiscal 1999 to 2000," said Nancy Wyman in her monthly letter on the state's finances.

The comptroller, who estimated that revenues from the personal income tax would outperform estimates by $185.2 million, while sales tax revenues would top projections by $60.1 million, said she was not raising her forecast for the surplus because the state's budget has yet to be finalized.

The state is predicting the surplus even though spending is expected to exceed the budget by $117.9 million. Medicaid, at $47.4 million, accounts for most of this rise, followed by Foster and Residential Care for Children under the Department of Children and families.

Using almost all of the surplus for spending or postponned revenue also means that the Connecticut will not be able to contribute to its Rainy Day fund, Wyman said, noting the governor, in his budget, said such deposits cannot be overstated. "Our economy is improving, but we can't say with certainity that these good times will last forever," she said.

Rowland plans to use $30.4 million of the fiscal 1997 surplus to pay one month's "capitated" Medicaid cost that otherwise would be paid in fiscal 1998. Another $34.9 million would be spent on accrued sick and vacation leave for an early retirement plant that has yet to be approved. And revenue from the sale of loan assets to the Connecticut Housing Finance Authority would be shifted to fiscal 1998 to 1999 from 1997.
